strategies.name: Continuous irrigated corn (current practice)
strategies.why: This is what most irrigated land here grows now. It is the baseline the other cards are compared with: irrigated corn uses the most pumped water of the grain crops (about 15 in/acre a year, reported to the state).

evidence.text: Kansas water-use reports, 2011-2025: single-crop irrigated corn points used a median 14.6 in/acre/yr across the region (year range 12.6-18.9), versus 10.3 for sorghum and 8.9 for wheat.
NASS county yields 2000-2018: irrigated corn yields varied about 12% (coefficient of variation) year to year, dryland corn about 47%.
At recent trends about 69% of Kansas High Plains aquifer storage could be used up within 50 years (model projection, not a measurement).
evidence.source: Steward, D.R. et al. (2013) Tapping unsustainable groundwater stores for agricultural production in the High Plains Aquifer of Kansas, projections to 2110. PNAS 110(37):E3477-E3486

benefits: Highest and most stable yields in most years
Familiar equipment, markets and crop insurance
gaps: Cost per acre uses USDA ERS Prairie Gateway averages that mix irrigated and dryland corn; pumping energy cost per acre-foot is not included (no citable source was reachable)
Irrigated yields after 2018 are estimated from the 2000-2018 irrigated/all-practice ratio because NASS stopped publishing them
risks: Uses the most water, so this field's clock runs fastest
Exposed to well-yield decline as saturated thickness falls: pumping capacity drops before the aquifer is 'empty'
strategies.soil_health: Continuous corn leaves a lot of residue, which protects the soil if it is kept on the surface; but a single crop keeps pest and disease cycles going and needs the most nitrogen.
strategies.yield_risk: Low while the well can keep up; rises sharply in drought years if well capacity has fallen.
strategies.applies_where: Everywhere with irrigation today (the current practice).

strategies.name: Corn-wheat-sorghum rotation with limited irrigation
strategies.why: Rotating corn with wheat and sorghum and capping irrigation spreads the water over crops that need less of it. Corn is limited to about 11 in/acre, the yearly average of the Sheridan-6 local enhanced management area (55 in over 5 years); wheat and sorghum get what farmers here report applying to them.

evidence.text: Kansas water-use reports: Sheridan County, which holds most of the Sheridan-6 LEMA (started 2013), reported 78,306 AF/yr of irrigation in 2008-2012 and 67,562 AF/yr in 2013-2017 (-14%); neighbouring Thomas County changed -4%. County totals include land outside the LEMA, and weather differs between the periods.

A satellite and statistics study of the Sheridan-6 LEMA reported that pumping fell by about a third with farmers shifting crops and irrigating less, at small cost to profit (unverified: we could not re-open the paper from the build environment).
evidence.source: Deines, J.M., Kendall, A.D., Butler, J.J. Jr., Hyndman, D.W. (2019) Quantifying irrigation adaptation strategies in response to stakeholder-driven groundwater management in the US High Plains Aquifer. Environ. Res. Lett. 14:044014 (unverified citation details)

evidence.text: WIMAS single-crop reports, 2011-2025 region medians: wheat 8.9 in/acre, sorghum 10.3 in/acre.

benefits: Cuts pumping substantially while keeping some irrigated income
Wheat and sorghum use their water at different times than corn, which can let one well cover more land
Breaks pest and disease cycles of continuous corn
gaps: Limited-irrigation corn yield is interpolated linearly between NASS irrigated and dryland yields; real yield response is usually less than linear (so income here is probably conservative)
ERS costs are not split by irrigation level
Rotation benefits to yield (rotation effect) are not included
risks: More management: three crops, three planting windows
Lower income than full corn in good price years
Wheat is exposed to spring freeze and hail
strategies.soil_health: A three-crop rotation with a winter crop keeps the ground covered more of the year than continuous corn and usually improves soil structure; less tillage helps keep that benefit.
strategies.yield_risk: Medium: limited water means drought years cut corn and sorghum yields more than under full irrigation.
strategies.applies_where: Fields with enough well capacity for limited irrigation; designed after the GMD4 Sheridan-6 LEMA.

strategies.name: Dryland wheat-sorghum-fallow
strategies.why: Going dryland stops pumping on this field entirely. Wheat-sorghum-fallow is the standard dryland rotation in western Kansas: the fallow year stores rain in the soil for the next crop.

evidence.text: NASS county yields 2000-2018: dryland wheat after fallow averaged about 97% of the all-practice county wheat yield, dryland sorghum about 92% of the all-practice sorghum yield.
NASS county yields 2000-2018: dryland wheat yields varied about 32% year to year (coefficient of variation) versus 12% for irrigated corn.

benefits: No pumping: the most years added to the clock
Keeps the water right's remaining water in the ground for later or for neighbours
gaps: The fallow year is counted with zero income and zero cost (weed-control cost in fallow is not included)
Crop insurance and government payments are not included
Converting a pivot to dryland has transition costs not modelled here
risks: Income falls a lot, and swings with rainfall
Fallow ground can blow in dry, windy springs if residue is low
Water-right rules: long non-use can affect a right (check with KDA-DWR)
strategies.soil_health: Fallow periods leave soil bare unless residue is kept (no-till); no-till fallow stores more water and reduces wind erosion. Dryland rotations add less organic matter than irrigated crops.
strategies.yield_risk: High: yields depend on rain; drought years can mean near-zero harvest.
strategies.applies_where: Anywhere, but best where saturated thickness is already thin or wells are weak.

strategies.name: Irrigated grain sorghum instead of corn
strategies.why: Grain sorghum is more drought tolerant than corn and here farmers report applying about 29% less water to it (10.3 vs 14.6 in/acre).

evidence.text: Kansas water-use reports, 2011-2025: sorghum 10.3 in/acre vs corn 14.6 in/acre (region medians of single-crop points).
MODIS satellite ET 2008-2024: sorghum fields evaporate about 1.1 in/yr less than corn fields (MODIS underestimates irrigated ET, so we use it only as a relative check).
evidence.source: NASA MODIS MOD16A3GF via Microsoft Planetary Computer

benefits: Uses less water with a similar machine setup to corn
gaps: Irrigated sorghum yields are scarce in NASS (county irrigated sorghum ends 2009); estimates rest on old ratios
ERS sorghum costs come from mostly dryland farms (about 4% of surveyed acres irrigated, ERS 2025)
risks: Lower price per bushel than corn and fewer nearby buyers
strategies.soil_health: Similar to corn; sorghum residue is durable and protects soil well.
strategies.yield_risk: Medium-low: sorghum keeps more yield than corn when water runs short.
strategies.applies_where: Most of the region; especially fields where well capacity has fallen.

strategies.name: Irrigated cotton instead of corn (southern counties)
strategies.why: Cotton is a warm-season crop that needs less irrigation than corn and is spreading into southwest Kansas. Points reporting cotton used about 10.1 in/acre.

evidence.text: Kansas water-use reports: cotton reported on irrigated points in 7 region counties in at least 5 years since 2011; 4,348 reported acres on average in 2021-2025.
Kansas cotton yields are only published at state level in recent years (NASS); income uses the state yield.

gaps: Few local cotton data: state yields, ERS Prairie Gateway costs, no county irrigated yields
Needs a gin within hauling distance (not assessed)
risks: Short growing season in the northern part of the region
strategies.soil_health: Cotton leaves little residue, so soil is more exposed to wind erosion; a cover or wheat rotation helps.
strategies.yield_risk: Medium: frost dates and hail; less known locally.
strategies.applies_where: Southern counties where farmers already report cotton (WIMAS); not recommended in the north.

method: Water: WIMAS reported application depth on single-crop irrigated points, county median of 2011-2025 (GMD acre-weighted value where a county has too few acres); limited-irrigation corn capped at 11 in/acre (Sheridan-6 LEMA allocation). Income: return over USDA ERS Prairie Gateway operating costs, USD per acre, median (and 10th-90th percentile) over 2016-2025 of county yield x Kansas price - cost for the same year. Irrigated / dryland yields = county all-practice yield x the county's 2000-2018 NASS practice ratio (NASS stopped county irrigated yields after 2018). Region values weight counties by irrigated corn acres (WIMAS groundwater acres x CDL corn share). Fallow years count as zero income and zero cost. Not included: pumping energy, insurance, government payments, transition costs. This is decision support, not a replacement for your agronomist.
